title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction
authors: Vipin Kurian Elavunkel, Sylvain Le Tonquesse, Hadrien Vroylandt
abstract: Identifying earth-abundant catalysts for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a central challenge in scalable green hydrogen production. We present a computational pipeline that couples diffusion-based generative modelling, machine-learning force-field relaxation, and graph neural network (GNN) property prediction to discover bimetallic HER catalysts beyond the structures and stoichiometries covered by existing adsorption databases. A generative model (MatterGen) is fine-tuned on bulk alloy structures labelled with their minimum hydrogen adsorption energy and steered towards adsorption energies near zero. From the generated pool we retain the stable structures that are novel bimetallic alloys: binary compositions built from the training-set metals but at stoichiometries or structures absent from that database. Each candidate's low-index facets are ranked by a machine-learning-force-field (MatterSim) surface-energy screen, and only the most stable terminations are converted into explicit slab models with hydrogen adsorbed at all high-symmetry surface sites and relaxed with the same force field. Two GNN surrogates (MEGNet and ALIGNN), trained on a high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) dataset, then screen the resulting slab candidates. Because the two models encode the local environment through different inductive biases, we retain only the alloys on which both agree, reducing the influence of any single model. This consensus screening, combined with a MatterSim energy-difference triangulation, resulted in a shortlist of near-thermoneutral bimetallic candidates. Eight are validated with plane-wave DFT, and four of them, Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3, bind hydrogen within the thermoneutral window. All eight alloys are dynamically stable by phonon calculations. These four alloys are highlighted as DFT-validated bimetallic HER candidates for experimental follow-up.

infographic.key_insight: Generative design and consensus GNN screening identified four DFT-validated bimetallic HER candidates with near-thermoneutral hydrogen binding: Pd5Au, Pt5Rh, Cu5Pt3, and Pd13Ru3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The pipeline narrows catalyst candidates for experimental follow-up while exploring alloy structures and stoichiometries beyond the training database.
method: Fine-tune MatterGen on adsorption-labelled bulk alloys to generate novel bimetallic structures targeting near-zero hydrogen adsorption energy.
Use MatterSim to rank low-index facets and relax hydrogen-covered slabs at high-symmetry adsorption sites.
Combine MEGNet–ALIGNN consensus with MatterSim energy-difference checks, then validate shortlisted alloys using DFT and phonons.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of eight alloys evaluated by plane-wave DFT, four bound hydrogen within the thermoneutral window; phonon calculations indicated all eight were dynamically stable.
infographic.watch_item: Near-thermoneutral binding is not experimental proof of HER performance, and all four highlighted candidates contain precious metals.
infographic.paper_title: Generative Design and Graph Neural Network Screening of Novel Bimetallic Alloy Catalysts for the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction

title: Quantum 3xplorer: AI-Native Engine for Next-Generation Quantum Materials Modeling
authors: Vsevolod Biryukov, Sergey V. Barabash, Pranab Kumar Das, Jack Deslippe, Mauro Del Ben, Felipe H. da Jornada
abstract: Quantum-mechanical approaches, such as density functional theory (DFT), underpin much of modern computational materials science and are the primary source of data for AI-driven discovery. Yet the established electronic-structure codes today represent decades-old software architectures, making new physical models slow and costly to implement, validate, and deploy on emerging hardware. We present Quantum 3xplorer (Q3, pronounced "Quantum Explorer"), an AI-native quantum simulation engine written from scratch by AI coding agents under the direction and supervision of domain scientists. As a first and demanding validation case, we implement plane-wave pseudopotential DFT end to end: norm-conserving, ultrasoft, and projector-augmented-wave formalisms, spin polarization, DFT+U, and dispersion corrections, together with forces, stresses, structural relaxation, and electronic-structure analysis. Q3 reproduces established reference implementations, runs faster on a single core in representative benchmarks, and scales across GPU-accelerated supercomputers. It was developed in weeks rather than years. Its layered, physics-first architecture separates abstract quantum-mechanical concepts from their numerical representations, making its framework extendable beyond plane waves to other basis sets and levels of theory. Its inputs and outputs follow structured, schema-validated data standards, making every result AI-ready. Q3 is open source under Apache 2.0 and built to be reused, extended, and improved by the research community. Q3 points to a paradigm shift in how computational quantum science is done. Scientists define the physics, formulate the models, and set the criteria for validation; AI agents write, test, and optimize the code. The decades-long path from a new theory to a trusted, high-performance implementation can thus collapse to days, significantly accelerating scientific discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum 3xplorer (Q3) demonstrates how scientist-supervised AI coding agents can build a quantum simulation engine in weeks rather than years.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its layered architecture, schema-validated data, and GPU scalability aim to simplify extending quantum models and integrating simulations into AI-driven materials workflows.
method: Scientists define physics and validation criteria; AI agents write, test, and optimize code.
Implement plane-wave pseudopotential DFT with multiple formalisms, forces, stresses, and structural relaxation.
Separate quantum concepts from numerical representations to support future extensions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement with established reference implementations, faster single-core execution in representative benchmarks, and scaling across GPU-accelerated supercomputers, but provides no numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Validation centers on plane-wave DFT; accuracy and performance for other basis sets or levels of theory remain to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum 3xplorer: AI-Native Engine for Next-Generation Quantum Materials Modeling

title: Crystoria: A Large-Scale Crystal Dataset Linking Thermodynamic and Dynamical Stability for Materials AI
authors: Ke-Xin Pang, Ze-Feng Gao, Yan Gao, Zhong-Yi Lu
abstract: Large-scale crystal databases have transformed materials discovery by making millions of structures and thermodynamic properties accessible to materials informatics. Yet dynamical stability remains sparsely characterized at a comparable scale because its evaluation is substantially more computationally demanding than conventional structure and energy calculations. This mismatch creates a critical gap between the rapidly expanding crystal-structure space and the physical information available for materials research and machine learning. Here we introduce Crystoria, a large-scale crystal dataset designed to bring dynamical stability to the scale of modern materials data. We construct Crystoria by systematically curating low-energy and metastable inorganic crystals, standardizing their structural identities, and combining machine-learning-accelerated structural relaxation with phonon-based dynamical screening. The resulting dataset contains 2,649,640 crystal structures, spanning 89 elements, 219 of the 230 space groups, and primitive cells containing 1-48 atoms. Among them, 1,793,353 structures (67.68%) are classified as dynamically stable, revealing substantial variation in dynamical stability across chemical and crystallographic space. By bringing dynamical stability to the scale of millions of crystal structures, Crystoria provides a physically grounded foundation for materials artificial intelligence (AI) and enables systematic exploration of the dynamical crystal landscape.

infographic.key_insight: Crystoria links thermodynamic and phonon-based dynamical stability information across 2.65 million crystal structures for materials AI.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The dataset can support AI screening of candidate materials beyond energy alone by incorporating dynamical stability.
method: Curate low-energy and metastable inorganic crystals and standardize structural identities.
Apply machine-learning-accelerated structural relaxation.
Screen dynamical stability using phonon calculations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Crystoria contains 2,649,640 structures spanning 89 elements, 219 space groups, and 1–48 atoms per primitive cell; 1,793,353 structures (67.68%) are classified as dynamically stable.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify phonon-screening thresholds or validation against higher-fidelity calculations, which are important when interpreting stability labels.
infographic.paper_title: Crystoria: A Large-Scale Crystal Dataset Linking Thermodynamic and Dynamical Stability for Materials AI

title: Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks
authors: Yunhong Han, Gaopeng Ren, Yan Liu, Ronghua Zhang, Huangjiang Huang, Ruiqi Zhang
abstract: Chemical kinetics determines molecular stability, reaction selectivity and the evolution of reacting mixtures, but discovering the underlying reaction networks remains challenging. Here we introduce ReactNexus, a generative framework for kinetic-guided network exploration starting solely from reactant graphs. Generative models propose transition states and predict the full reaction trajectories connecting reactants and products, while calculations using a machine-learned interatomic potential verify connectivity and evaluate electronic barriers. On an in-distribution benchmark of 10,000 generated candidates, 80.8% connect to the input reactant after density functional theory (DFT) optimization and intrinsic reaction coordinate verification. The resulting networks uncover lower-barrier cooperative pathways and competition between catalyst release and catalyst-bound branches. In the examined carbocation cascades, coverage of known product precursors saturates after limited expansion and distinct entries converge onto shared intermediates, indicating a compact accessible reaction space. Network-derived candidate structures further assist mass-spectral interpretation of a complex nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction. Together, these results establish a generative approach to reaction-network discovery and mechanistic analysis without predefined products or reaction templates.

infographic.key_insight: ReactNexus discovers kinetically informed chemical reaction networks from reactant graphs without predefined products or reaction templates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can help engineers explore competing reaction pathways, identify lower-barrier routes, and interpret complex reaction mixtures.
method: Generate candidate transition states and full reaction trajectories from reactant graphs.
Use a machine-learned interatomic potential to verify connectivity and evaluate electronic barriers.
Expand reaction networks to reveal shared intermediates and competing branches.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an in-distribution benchmark of 10,000 generated candidates, 80.8% connected to the input reactant after DFT optimization and intrinsic reaction coordinate verification.
infographic.watch_item: The reported connectivity rate is in-distribution and does not establish network completeness or generalization to unfamiliar chemistry.
infographic.paper_title: Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks

title: ORCHID: Connecting Finite-Temperature Thermodynamic Evidence to Computational Materials Discovery
authors: Raymundo Arróyave, James E. Saal, Dongwon Shin
abstract: Finite-temperature phase stability is essential to materials discovery, but the evidence needed to describe it remains scattered across decades of literature. ORCHID organizes this evidence around the thermodynamic states that the observations describe, using tiered agentic extraction guided by thermodynamic rules, expert supervision and explicit validation. The collection contains 73,542 values from 1,321 papers, represented with their thermodynamic states, phase identities, provenance, evidence classes and uncertainty, together with assessed phase assemblages and calculated references. A qualified subset is released in ESPEI-compatible form for CALPHAD assessment, and machine-readable access supports both human and AI-assisted reuse. Blind expert evaluation of 48 diagram fields gives 93.8% agreement, increasing to 97.9% after accounting for notation conventions. On a common formation-enthalpy benchmark, eight MLIPs show residual spreads close to their DFT reference, motivating evaluation of finite-temperature phase stability through PhaseForge. One-shot MLIP-PhaseForge descriptions of Cu-Zr recover 0.35-0.56 of observed phase occurrences at assessed field points. ORCHID-assisted refinement through PhaseForge+ recovers 9 of 13 invariant temperatures within 2 sigma and reduces held-out activity error from 5.1 to 1.7 kJ/mol. By supplying interpreted literature evidence directly to gradient-based refinement through PhaseForge+, ORCHID connects evidence recovery to programmatic CALPHAD assessment. With the initial description and fitting datasets prepared, the final Cu-Zr refinement completes in approximately 27 minutes, providing a foundation for continuously updated thermodynamic models and their use in materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: ORCHID connects literature-derived finite-temperature thermodynamic evidence to programmatic CALPHAD refinement for materials discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structured, traceable thermodynamic evidence can help engineers refine phase-stability models and evaluate materials under finite-temperature conditions.
method: Extract literature evidence using tiered agents, thermodynamic rules, expert supervision and explicit validation.
Organize values by thermodynamic state, phase identity, provenance, evidence class and uncertainty; export a qualified subset for ESPEI.
Evaluate MLIP-based phase stability with PhaseForge and refine thermodynamic descriptions using ORCHID evidence through PhaseForge+.

infographic.watch_item: The approximately 27-minute Cu–Zr refinement excludes preparation of the initial description and fitting datasets, and broader system-level generalization remains to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: ORCHID: Connecting Finite-Temperature Thermodynamic Evidence to Computational Materials Discovery

title: Agentic Global Optimization of Site-Disordered Crystalline Materials
authors: Martin Hoffmann Petersen, Zekun Ren, Kedar Hippalgaonkar
abstract: Site-disordered crystals, in which several elements partially occupy the same atomic site, cannot be simulated atomistically without first resolving an explicit ordering, and the number of possible orderings grows combinatorially with supercell size. Because each candidate requires an expensive structural relaxation, locating the global-minimum ordering is a costly combinatorial search. Here, we present an agentic search in which a surrogate model, fitted to previously evaluated configurations, selects each subsequent candidate by balancing exploitation, uncertainty, and novelty. Four surrogates are implemented within a shared framework: an ExtraTrees ensemble, Bayesian ridge regression, sparse ARD regression, and an ALiEGNN-inspired graph ensemble. These are benchmarked against three traditional methods: random walk, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and a genetic algorithm across 14 test cases spanning 12 crystal structures, with exhaustively enumerated global minima as ground truth. The agentic surrogates reach the global minimum in 94% of runs, compared with 55% for the traditional methods, with a median 4.3-fold reduction in evaluations relative to the best traditional method. Bayesian ridge regression succeeds in all runs with the fewest evaluations. Applied to Na2/3FePO4, with coupled Na/vacancy configurational disorder and Fe2+/Fe3+ charge disorder, the framework recovers the experimentally reported ordering when charge states are encoded in the surrogate representation, demonstrating its extension to multi-sublattice disorder.

infographic.key_insight: Surrogate-guided agentic search finds low-energy atomic orderings in site-disordered crystals more reliably and with fewer costly evaluations than traditional search methods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can reduce the structural-relaxation workload needed to model chemically disordered crystalline materials.
method: Fit a surrogate to evaluated configurations and select new candidates by balancing exploitation, uncertainty, and novelty.
Compare ExtraTrees, Bayesian ridge, sparse ARD, and an ALiEGNN-inspired graph ensemble against three traditional search methods.
Encode coupled Na/vacancy and Fe charge-state disorder to model Na2/3FePO4.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 14 test cases spanning 12 crystal structures with exhaustively verified global minima, agentic surrogates succeeded in 94% of runs versus 55% for traditional methods, with a median 4.3-fold reduction in evaluations relative to the best traditional method.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on larger, non-enumerable search spaces remains unverified; recovering the reported Na2/3FePO4 ordering required explicit charge-state encoding.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Global Optimization of Site-Disordered Crystalline Materials

title: Full-Potential Korringa Kohn Rostoker Study of Structural and Mechanical Properties in SiGeSn Alloys
authors: Wasim Raja Mondal, Swarnava Ghosh, Ka-Ming Tam, Markus Eisenbach, Yang Wang, Hanna Terletska
abstract: Accurate first-principles descriptions of open, covalently bonded crystal structures remain challenging within conventional Korringa--Kohn--Rostoker (KKR) approaches owing to the spherical approximations commonly employed for the effective crystal potential. Here, we systematically assess the recently developed full-potential KKR (KKR-FP) implementation in the open-source MuST package and demonstrate its applicability to diamond-structured group-IV semiconductors and SiGeSn alloys. Benchmark calculations for diamond-structured Si reveal substantial limitations of the conventional muffin-tin and atomic sphere approximations, whereas KKR-FP accurately reproduces the experimental equilibrium lattice parameter and bulk modulus, yielding 5.433 and 94.9 GPa. The full-potential treatment also recovers the semiconducting character of Si. Further calculations for elemental Ge and Sn establish the applicability of the approach across group-IV materials. Extending this framework to SiGeSn alloys, we investigate their composition-dependent equilibrium lattice parameters, bulk moduli, and mixing enthalpies. The calculated lattice parameters exhibit positive deviations from Vegard's law, while the bulk modulus decreases substantially with changes in alloy composition. Moreover, positive mixing enthalpies of 180.92 and 346.32 meV/atom are obtained for Si0.5Ge0.375Sn0.125 and Si0.375Ge0.25Sn0.375, respectively, indicating an energetic penalty for homogeneous alloy formation relative to the selected elemental reference states. These findings highlight the importance of nonspherical potential contributions in accurately describing open-structured semiconductors and establish KKR-FP within MuST as a promising framework for investigating the structural properties and mixing energetics of compositionally complex group-IV alloys

infographic.key_insight: Full-potential KKR accurately describes diamond-structured Si and predicts composition-dependent structural properties and unfavorable mixing energetics in SiGeSn alloys.
infographic.engineering_relevance: KKR-FP in MuST offers a first-principles framework for assessing lattice compatibility, stiffness, and alloying energetics in group-IV semiconductor materials.
method: Benchmark full-potential KKR against muffin-tin and atomic sphere approximations for Si.
Extend calculations to elemental Ge and Sn.
Calculate SiGeSn equilibrium lattice parameters, bulk moduli, and mixing enthalpies.
infographic.evidence_signal: For Si, KKR-FP yields an equilibrium lattice parameter of 5.433 Å and bulk modulus of 94.9 GPa; two SiGeSn compositions have positive mixing enthalpies of 180.92 and 346.32 meV/atom.
infographic.watch_item: Positive mixing enthalpies are relative to selected elemental reference states and do not alone establish finite-temperature alloy stability.
infographic.paper_title: Full-Potential Korringa Kohn Rostoker Study of Structural and Mechanical Properties in SiGeSn Alloys

title: Framework-Conditional Open Materials Generation
authors: Maya M. Martirossyan, Hillary Pan, Philipp Höllmer, Stefano Martiniani
abstract: Theoretical predictions of novel materials rely on a variety of techniques, from data-mining-based ion substitution methods to fully de novo generative models. Each approach imposes specific constraints and encounters unique challenges when extrapolating beyond the distribution of known materials to discover new ones. The foremost goal of materials generation is to produce stable, unique, and novel (S.U.N.) structures. Predicted structures that meet these criteria, however, typically result from novel chemical compositions mapped onto known structural prototypes or frameworks. We leverage this heuristic insight to present a new generative paradigm for the de novo prediction of inorganic crystalline materials constrained by their structural framework---i.e., the unit cell shapes and respective particle positions. Our method, termed OMatG-FC (Open Materials Framework-Conditional Generation), learns via a combination of discrete flow matching on the atomic species and stochastic interpolants for the volume scaling of the unit cell lattice, while fixing in-place the fractional coordinates and the unit-volume lattice vectors, dramatically reducing the dimensionality of the problem compared to unconstrained (framework-free) generation. Our method is more flexible than existing prototype-constrained methods, demonstrating capability for discovery of unseen, stable prototypes derived from known structural frameworks. We also investigate the number of unique frameworks in the MP-20 dataset, demonstrating the propensity of duplicate frameworks within the dataset and providing a framework-split version. We benchmark the performance of our model using the LeMat-GenBench suite using three ML interatomic potentials and achieve state-of-the-art S.U.N. rate below the convex hull, eschewing the need to learn atomic packings for materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: OMatG-FC generates new inorganic crystals by learning atomic identities and unit-cell volume while keeping the structural framework fixed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Framework conditioning reduces the generation problem’s dimensionality, enabling materials discovery without learning atomic packings from scratch.
method: Fix fractional atomic coordinates and unit-volume lattice vectors.
Generate atomic species using discrete flow matching and scale lattice volume using stochastic interpolants.
Audit duplicate frameworks in MP-20 and provide a framework-split dataset.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation with LeMat-GenBench and three ML interatomic potentials reports a state-of-the-art stable, unique, and novel (S.U.N.) rate below the convex hull, though the abstract gives no numerical rate.
infographic.watch_item: Fixed input frameworks constrain the structural search space, and ML-predicted stability requires higher-fidelity validation.
infographic.paper_title: Framework-Conditional Open Materials Generation

title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?
authors: Ruoyu Wu, Zengji Tu, Aolong Sun, Tianyi Ma, Junren Li, Xinbo Xu
abstract: Before AI can be trusted to discover new science, it should be able to reproduce what science already knows. Reproduction provides a rigorous checkpoint for an AI scientist: the target claim is known, yet recovering it still requires translating an incomplete scientific description into an executable experiment and producing evidence that can be independently verified. Existing research-reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, where experiments share relatively homogeneous software stacks. Extending this capability across scientific disciplines introduces a different challenge: agents must operate domain-specific scientific software, make physical and numerical choices, diagnose long-running computations, and distinguish valid evidence from merely plausible outputs. We introduce PAPERBENCHX, a benchmark of 93 expert-constructed paper-reproduction tasks spanning 12 research areas across electromagnetics, photonics, chemistry, materials science, biology, and robotics. Each task provides the source paper, a public task specification, and a domain-native scientific environment involving specialized scientific software. Agents must reconstruct a key experiment, execute and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow that supports the target scientific claim. To evaluate scientific validity rather than surface-level agreement, we replay every submission from scratch and score only regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria. Across 10 frontier agent configurations, the best configuration fully reproduces only 14% tasks under the 90% threshold. Meanwhile, mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08%, indicating that substantial partial progress rarely translates into complete scientific reproduction. These results reveal a large gap between paper understanding and reliably producing reproducible scientific evidence.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents make substantial partial progress on scientific reproduction, but the best tested configuration fully reproduced only 14% of tasks at a 90% scoring threshold.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable AI-assisted materials research requires executable workflows, sound physical and numerical choices, and independently regenerated evidence—not just plausible outputs.
method: Construct 93 expert-designed paper-reproduction tasks spanning 12 research areas.
Provide source papers, task specifications, and domain-native scientific software environments.
Replay submissions from scratch and score regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 10 frontier agent configurations, mean rubric scores ranged from 27.53% to 59.08%, while the best configuration achieved only 14% full reproduction.
infographic.watch_item: Results span multiple disciplines and should not be interpreted as a materials-science-specific success rate.
infographic.paper_title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?

title: Query-Efficient Quantum Multi-Objective Optimization for Materials Configuration Search via Bayesian Weight Selection
authors: Onur Boyar, Seiji Takeda, Akihiro Kosugi, Indra Priyadarsini S, Lisa Hamada, Sina Klampt
abstract: Materials design is a multi-objective problem, and recent advances in quantum optimization make it possible to bring quantum solvers to bear on such problems. The realistic near-term win, though, is not raw quantum advantage but making an expensive, noisy quantum solver usable by spending its calls wisely. Quantum Approximate Multi-Objective Optimization (QAMOO) traces a Pareto front by solving a family of scalarized Ising problems, one per objective-weight vector, with QAOA --- but chooses those weights \emph{non-adaptively}, sampling them at random, blind to what it has already found. We recast weight selection as \emph{multi-objective Bayesian optimization}: our method, BW-QAMOO (Bayes-Weighted QAMOO), picks each next weight by expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) under a Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate over the weight-to-objective map. On a frustrated alloy-configuration benchmark across $m\in\{3,4\}$ objectives and $n\in\{10,11,12\}$ sites, BW-QAMOO reaches the same Pareto hypervolume as QAMOO's random sampling with a median 33% fewer scalarized solves across the 90/95\% targets and 60--74\% fewer than a uniform-grid baseline), on a genuine (simulated) QAOA solver; a paired Wilcoxon test confirms the saving is significant, and the advantage grows with the objective count m as the weight simplex expands and blind sampling wastes more of the budget. This is a \emph{query-efficiency} result, and we close with the open challenges on the path to real alloy data and hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive Bayesian weight selection helps quantum multi-objective optimization reach comparable Pareto coverage with fewer costly solver calls.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reducing scalarized solves could make limited quantum-computing budgets more useful for exploring competing materials-design objectives.
method: BW-QAMOO learns a Gaussian-process surrogate mapping objective weights to objective outcomes.
Expected hypervolume improvement selects the next weight vector adaptively.
QAOA solves the resulting scalarized Ising problems to expand Pareto coverage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across frustrated alloy benchmarks with 3–4 objectives and 10–12 sites, simulated QAOA required a median 33% fewer solves than random sampling at 90%/95% hypervolume targets and 60–74% fewer than a uniform grid; a paired Wilcoxon test supported the savings.
infographic.watch_item: This demonstrates query efficiency, not quantum advantage; validation on real alloy data and quantum hardware remains open.
infographic.paper_title: Query-Efficient Quantum Multi-Objective Optimization for Materials Configuration Search via Bayesian Weight Selection

title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields
authors: Wenbo Fu, Chenghui Mao, Chengwen Hu, Haifeng Lv, Zhou Lv
abstract: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/angstrom; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.

infographic.key_insight: Radial Kernel Attention enables linear-cost global feature exchange, improving energy and force prediction for polymer-derived clusters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RKA offers a compact way to capture interactions beyond local neighbor graphs without the quadratic cost of all-pair attention.
method: Map atomic distances from the cluster centroid into learned radial features.
Combine radial-feature overlap with content-dependent queries and keys using factorized aggregation.
Insert invariant scalar updates between EquiformerV3 local blocks and differentiate total energy to obtain conservative forces.
infographic.evidence_signal: After 12 training epochs on OPoly26, complete official validation-split evaluation showed 67.4% lower per-atom energy MAE and 36.3% lower force MAE in a matched 5M-model comparison; the 20M RKA model achieved 15.81 meV total-energy MAE and 2.619 meV/angstrom force MAE.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover finite polymer-derived clusters; performance on periodic bulk polymers and stability in long molecular-dynamics trajectories remain unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Radial Kernel Attention for Long-Range Modeling in Polymer Machine Learning Force Fields

title: SKFitter: Symmetry resolved Slater Koster tight-binding models from first principles for s, p, d and f electrons, spin orbit coupling and magnetism
authors: Sundeep Kapila, Bhaskaran Muralidharan, Satadeep Bhattacharjee
abstract: Constructing accurate and physically interpretable tight binding (TB) Hamiltonians from first principles calculations remains challenging, particularly for materials exhibiting complex orbital hybridization, spin orbit coupling (SOC), and magnetic order. SKFitter is an open-source Python framework for constructing and optimizing symmetry resolved Slater Koster TB models directly from density functional theory (DFT) calculations performed using Quantum ESPRESSO or VASP. The framework supports s to f orbitals, incorporates on site SOC and site resolved magnetic exchange interactions, and accommodates both orthogonal and nonorthogonal basis. A central feature is the symmetry resolved parameterization of orbital manifolds, which allows independent two centre hopping integrals between symmetry allowed orbital groups and across distinct neighbour shells. SKFitter also identifies missing orbital contributions and guide systematic basis set refinement and optimizes parameters through weights. The resulting Hamiltonian can be used to evaluate anomalous (AHC) and spin Hall conductivities (SHC), and topological invariants. We demonstrate the framework using eight representative materials spanning semimetals, semiconductors, transition metals, f-electron compounds, and magnetic systems. Symmetry resolved models achieve band energy errors of 9 to 41 meV within 1 eV of the Fermi level. The fitted Hamiltonians reproduce characteristic features of the SHC response of Pt, the SOC dependence of the AHC of Fe, and the momentum dependent altermagnetic spin splitting of MnTe without any altermagnet specific interaction. For EuMn2Bi2, projection guided orbital refinement reduces the near Fermi level fitting error from 120 to 32 meV. Together, these results establish SKFitter as a flexible and reproducible framework for developing symmetry consistent, physically interpretable TB models of complex materials.

infographic.key_insight: SKFitter converts first-principles calculations into symmetry-resolved, physically interpretable tight-binding models that capture complex orbital, spin–orbit, and magnetic effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The open-source Python framework enables compact electronic-structure models for evaluating spin transport, magnetic responses, and topological properties.
method: Fit symmetry-resolved Slater–Koster parameters to Quantum ESPRESSO or VASP calculations.
Support s–f orbitals, on-site spin–orbit coupling, site-resolved exchange, and orthogonal or nonorthogonal bases.
Refine orbital bases using projection diagnostics and optimize fits with weighting.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight representative materials, reported band-energy errors are 9–41 meV within 1 eV of the Fermi level; orbital refinement reduces the EuMn2Bi2 near-Fermi error from 120 to 32 meV.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on orbital-basis selection and fitting weights; near-Fermi band agreement alone does not establish accuracy for all derived responses.
infographic.paper_title: SKFitter: Symmetry resolved Slater Koster tight-binding models from first principles for s, p, d and f electrons, spin orbit coupling and magnetism

title: Resisting Drying Stress in Laponite Bentonite Clay Composites, Two Step Yielding and Crack Peel Selection
authors: Tapati Dutta, Agnishikha Chakrabarti, Soham Mitra, Deepshikha Das, Indranil Chakraborty
abstract: Clay films that dry on a rigid substrate crack, peel or stay intact, and which of these happens matters for coatings, barrier layers and ceramic processing. Composites of clay with polymers have been studied widely. Clay composites, whose components differ in size and charge, are much less explored. We show that mixing the nano scale clay Laponite with the micron scale clay Bentonite reduces desiccation damage on both a hydrophobic and a hydrophilic substrate, Laponite films stay essentially intact, Bentonite films fracture extensively, and on glass most intermediate compositions are less damaged than a simple average of the two would suggest. Rheology of the gelled suspensions reveals a two step yielding in every composition, and the cohesive energy derived from it depends by orders of magnitude on which step is used, a point that any rheology cracking correlation must specify. A dimensionless cohesion adhesion index, whose sign we derive from an energy balance, is consistent with compositions that peel on polypropylene and crack on glass. Replicate experiments were performed for robustness of results. The results identify composition as a simple handle on the crack resistance of clay films and open the search for the critical crack-free thickness as a function of clay composition.

infographic.key_insight: Mixing nanoscale Laponite with microscale Bentonite reduces drying damage, with most intermediate compositions on glass outperforming a simple average of the pure-clay endpoints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Clay composition offers a practical way to improve drying resistance in coatings, barrier layers and ceramic processing.
method: Compare drying damage across clay compositions on hydrophobic polypropylene and hydrophilic glass.

title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models
authors: Pengfei Cai, Katharina S. C. Jäger, Utkarsh Utkarsh, Nofit Segal, Bowen Deng, Akshay Subramanian
abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models offer scalable approaches to generating crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes. However, satisfying crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry, and accurate stereochemistry remains challenging. Satisfying these requirements calls for corrections that preserve the geometry already captured by the pretrained model. In this work, we propose AtomSteer, a test-time inference framework for steering pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints. During sampling, AtomSteer corrects intermediate structure predictions with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. We demonstrate AtomSteer across three pretrained backbones, FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, spanning de novo crystal generation and crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation and improves target space-group recovery in crystal structure prediction. AtomSteer improves molecular validity and E/Z stereochemical accuracy while retaining conformer ensemble fidelity. For protein-ligand complexes, AtomSteer reduces ligand E/Z errors relative to experimental reference structures while achieving competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity. Our method provides a unified framework for adding chemical and crystallographic control to existing atomistic generative models without retraining or architectural changes.

infographic.key_insight: AtomSteer steers pretrained atomistic generative models toward chemical and crystallographic constraints at inference time, without retraining or architectural changes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It adds structural control to existing workflows for crystal design, molecular conformer generation, and protein–ligand structure prediction while limiting disruption to generated geometry.
method: Correct intermediate predictions during sampling using bounded local projections.
Apply graph-rigid stereochemical transformations and periodic-symmetry projections.
Accept updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes elsewhere.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, the abstract reports improved crystal symmetry coverage and recovery, molecular validity and E/Z accuracy, and fewer ligand E/Z errors with competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify inference overhead or improvement magnitudes, leaving the practical cost–benefit trade-off unclear.
infographic.paper_title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models

title: First-Principles Identification of Higher-Order Configurational Energy Terms and Their Magnetic-State Dependence in Lithium-Rich Oxyfluorides: From QUBO to HUBO
authors: Joonho Bae
abstract: In this work, we use spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) to identify substantial third-order, nonadditive configurational energy contributions in lithium-rich oxyfluorides that quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models cannot represent. We test the extension from QUBO to higher-order unconstrained binary optimization (HUBO) in two disordered-rocksalt cathode materials, Li$_2$MnO$_2$F (LMOF) and Li$_2$Mn$_{0.5}$Ti$_{0.5}$O$_2$F (LMTiOF), using composition-preserving DFT energy maps. Using fixed-geometry energy maps, we show that cubic HUBO captures nonadditive contributions absent from QUBO models and substantially reduces fitting errors in both materials. Direct DFT energy differences confirm third-order nonadditivity, while comparisons of magnetic initializations reveal a strong dependence of the LMTiOF contribution on the converged electronic state. These results support the inclusion of higher-order terms when modeling configurational energetics and highlight the need to account for magnetic-state dependence in constructing DFT energy maps. The extracted terms describe effective couplings among composition-preserving exchange variables, rather than uniquely identified microscopic three-atom interactions.

infographic.key_insight: Cubic HUBO captures substantial third-order configurational energy contributions that quadratic QUBO models miss in lithium-rich oxyfluorides.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Higher-order energy models could improve configurational modeling of disordered-rocksalt cathodes, provided magnetic-state dependence is accounted for.
method: Compute composition-preserving, fixed-geometry energy maps using spin-polarized DFT.
Compare QUBO and cubic HUBO fits for Li₂MnO₂F and Li₂Mn₀.₅Ti₀.₅O₂F.
Test third-order nonadditivity with direct DFT energy differences and compare magnetic initializations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Cubic HUBO substantially reduces fitting errors in both materials, while direct DFT energy differences confirm third-order nonadditivity and reveal strong electronic-state dependence in Li₂Mn₀.₅Ti₀.₅O₂F.
infographic.watch_item: The fitted terms are effective couplings among composition-preserving exchange variables, not uniquely identified microscopic three-atom interactions.
infographic.paper_title: First-Principles Identification of Higher-Order Configurational Energy Terms and Their Magnetic-State Dependence in Lithium-Rich Oxyfluorides: From QUBO to HUBO

title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
authors: Edgar Josué Landinez Borda, Ravindra Shinde, Claudia Filippi, Markus Holzmann, Saverio Moroni
abstract: We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.

infographic.key_insight: Multideterminant QMC barely changes excitation energies but is crucial for capturing exciton localization in low-density solid molecular hydrogen.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate localization is needed to predict optical transition strengths and excitation-induced forces, which excitation energies alone may not reliably characterize.
method: Model phase-I molecular hydrogen under increasing compression using QMC.
Compare single-orbital substitutions with multideterminant expansions covering all single particle–hole transitions.
Benchmark against BSE and TDDFT across nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Multideterminant QMC generally agrees with BSE on localization, transition dipoles, and excitation-induced forces, while TDDFT predicts more extended excitons; differences diminish under compression.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement depends on nuclear configuration, with marked QMC–BSE discrepancies where predicted exciton localization differs substantially.
infographic.paper_title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo

title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica: effect of passivation, orientation and load
authors: Enrico Pedretti, Maria Clelia Righi
abstract: Friction and wear of diamond are controlled by its surface chemistry, which determines whether covalent bonds form across the sliding interface. First-principles simulations have explored the role of surface orientation and passivation, but are limited to a few hundred atoms and tens of picoseconds. To bridge this gap, we develop a reactive machine learning interatomic potential for the C/H/N/O/Si chemical space, covering diamond, silicon nitride, silicon oxide, their surfaces, interfaces, and environmental molecules. The potential is trained on a large dataset of diverse structures and is tested on multiple physical properties, including ab initio reaction barriers on diamond surfaces, and structural/mechanical properties of amorphous Si$_3$N$_4$ and SiO$_2$. We then simulate sliding of diamond-Si$_3$N$_4$ interfaces with four surface orientations, clean and H/OH-passivated terminations, and normal loads from 0.1 to 23 GPa. We identify two different regimes: one where sliding is localized at the interface, and shear stress is proportional to the interfacial bond density, and another where shear is distributed inside the softer material, and adhesion due to full interfacial bonding dominates. These results show how passivation, surface orientation and load together determine interfacial bonding and friction, with implications for the environmental sensitivity of diamond wear. More broadly, the potential enables reactive simulations of diamond, silicon nitride and silica with near-ab initio accuracy at length and time scales beyond first-principles methods, providing a useful tool for future studies of wear at plowing asperities, chemical-mechanical polishing, and properties of amorphous ceramic films.

infographic.key_insight: Diamond–silicon nitride friction shifts from bond-density-controlled interfacial sliding to shear within the softer material as passivation, crystal orientation and load alter interfacial bonding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The potential enables larger-scale reactive simulations to investigate diamond wear, chemical-mechanical polishing and ceramic interfaces beyond first-principles simulation limits.
method: Train a reactive machine learning potential for C/H/N/O/Si across bulk materials, surfaces, interfaces and environmental molecules.
Test diamond surface reaction barriers and amorphous silicon nitride and silica structural/mechanical properties.
Simulate diamond–silicon nitride sliding across four diamond orientations, clean and H/OH-passivated surfaces, and 0.1–23 GPa normal loads.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports training on a large, diverse structural dataset and evaluation against ab initio reaction barriers and amorphous-material properties, but provides no numerical accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability to wear, plowing asperities and silica sliding requires further validation; the reported sliding study focuses on diamond–silicon nitride.
infographic.paper_title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica: effect of passivation, orientation and load

title: Magnetic crystal generation with site-resolved magnetic moments via Gaussian-mixture retargeting and finite-budget yield prediction
authors: Wen-Chuang Shang, Chenyu Shen, Mikito Tsujimoto, Tomonori Tanaka, Yoshihiro Gohda
abstract: We introduce GMMag, a workflow for generating crystal structures together with their site-resolved magnetic moments, built on a conditional variational autoencoder with a graph neural network encoder and a transformer decoder. Gaussian-mixture sampling redirects generation towards selected chemical and magnetic targets without retraining. We systematically investigate how encoder and decoder design, the representation of magnetic-moment magnitudes and relative signs, and sampling choices affect reconstruction, generation quality and diversity. Because a higher screening pass rate does not necessarily yield more qualifying candidates with distinct chemical formulas absent from the reference dataset, we model how repeated generation of the same chemical formulas limits their accumulation and test the model in two separate ten-million-draw runs. As an application, the workflow identifies Nd-containing candidates with chemical formulas absent from the reference dataset, negative formation energies and high estimated saturation magnetization.

infographic.key_insight: GMMag generates crystal structures with site-resolved magnetic moments and retargets generation toward chemical and magnetic goals using Gaussian-mixture sampling without retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports magnetic-material candidate discovery while estimating how duplicate chemical formulas limit distinct-candidate yield under a finite sampling budget.
method: Combine a graph-neural-network encoder with a transformer decoder in a conditional variational autoencoder.
Use Gaussian-mixture sampling to target selected chemical and magnetic properties.
Model repeated-formula generation to predict accumulation of qualifying formulas absent from the reference dataset.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study compares architecture, magnetic-moment representations and sampling choices, tests yield prediction in two separate ten-million-draw runs, and identifies Nd-containing candidates with negative formation energies and high estimated saturation magnetization.
infographic.watch_item: Absence from the reference dataset does not establish global novelty, and estimated magnetic performance requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Magnetic crystal generation with site-resolved magnetic moments via Gaussian-mixture retargeting and finite-budget yield prediction

title: First-Principles Investigation of Irida-Graphane: A Wide-Band-Gap Semiconductor Derived from Irida-Graphene
authors: Djardiel S. Gomes, Isaac M. Félix, Marcelo L. Pereira Junior
abstract: Opening a band gap in metallic two-dimensional carbon allotropes is an important step toward their use in electronic and optoelectronic devices, and full hydrogenation has proven to be an effective route to achieve it. Here, we propose irida-graphane, the fully hydrogenated derivative of the irida-graphene, a monolayer composed of three-, six-, and eight-membered rings, and investigate its structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties using density functional theory (DFT) at the PBE and HSE06 levels combined with phonon and \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. All carbon atoms adopt $sp^3$ hybridization, with the hydrogen atoms of the three- and six-membered rings bonded to opposite sides of a buckled carbon framework, and the lattice parameter contracts by 4.3% with respect to irida-graphene. The hydrogenation energy of $-0.53$ eV/H indicates that the hydrogenation of irida-graphene from molecular hydrogen is exothermic. The absence of imaginary phonon frequencies confirms the dynamical stability of irida-graphane, and AIMD simulations show that its structure remains intact at temperatures up to 2000 K. Irida-graphane is mechanically isotropic, with an in-plane stiffness of approximately 156 N/m, a Poisson's ratio of approximately 0.1, and critical strains of approximately 20%. Hydrogenation transforms the metallic parent structure into a semiconductor with an indirect band gap of 4.68 eV (PBE) and 6.0 eV (HSE06). Irida-graphane is transparent in the visible range, with reflectivity below 0.3%, and absorbs strongly in the deep ultraviolet, with absorption coefficients of the order of $10^{5} - 10^{6}$ cm$^{-1}$. These results suggest irida-graphane as a candidate wide-gap material for ultraviolet optoelectronics and transparent coatings.

infographic.key_insight: First-principles calculations predict that full hydrogenation converts metallic irida-graphene into irida-graphane, an indirect wide-band-gap semiconductor with a 6.0 eV HSE06 gap.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicted visible transparency and strong deep-ultraviolet absorption make irida-graphane a candidate for UV optoelectronics and transparent coatings.
method: PBE and HSE06 density functional theory calculations
Phonon analysis and ab initio molecular dynamics
Structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical characterization
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations show no imaginary phonon frequencies, structural integrity in AIMD up to 2000 K, visible reflectivity below 0.3%, and deep-UV absorption coefficients of 10⁵–10⁶ cm⁻¹.
infographic.watch_item: The predictions require experimental validation, particularly synthesis with complete hydrogenation and the proposed hydrogen arrangement.
infographic.paper_title: First-Principles Investigation of Irida-Graphane: A Wide-Band-Gap Semiconductor Derived from Irida-Graphene

title: FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D
authors: Feng Chen, Jianguo Huang, Yushan Xiao, Yue Li, Bijun Tang, Xuyu Dong
abstract: To accelerate materials discovery, language models must be able to address problems at the research frontier. Yet textbook- and examination-derived benchmarks primarily assess established knowledge, leaving performance on frontier research problems largely untested. We introduce FrontierMat, a benchmark of 330 problems drawn from frontier academic and industrial research in fields including aerospace, semiconductors, embodied intelligence and nuclear fusion. Every problem is validated by leading experimentalists and industry experts in its field. Each problem presents a real study and asks the model to infer a withheld outcome or draw a conclusion from selected experimental evidence. Problems are annotated by functional domain, material system and the scale of the governing mechanism; 130 require cross-scale reasoning. The strongest general-purpose model scores only 53.7%, and on matched problems, cross-scale problems score 8.7 points below single-scale ones. Half of the problems are solved by at most one model, and models fail chiefly by endorsing what is plausible rather than what was observed. A domain-adaptation study with meta-weighted continued pretraining and scale-modular self-distillation raises an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%, matching the strongest proprietary model, with improvements on public materials benchmarks and no decline in aggregate performance on general benchmarks. FrontierMat provides a testbed for measuring progress toward language models that support frontier materials R&D.

infographic.key_insight: FrontierMat exposes a gap between plausible answers and experimentally grounded reasoning in frontier materials R&D.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark tests whether language models can infer research outcomes from experimental evidence, including mechanisms spanning multiple scales.
method: Build 330 expert-validated problems from frontier academic and industrial studies.
Annotate functional domain, material system and mechanism scale; include 130 cross-scale problems.
Adapt an open-weight model using meta-weighted continued pretraining and scale-modular self-distillation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The strongest general-purpose model scores 53.7%; cross-scale problems score 8.7 percentage points below matched single-scale problems, while domain adaptation raises an open-weight model from 36.7% to 55.4%.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark gains do not establish reliability in live R&D; experimentally plausible but incorrect conclusions remain a key risk.
infographic.paper_title: FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D
